title: Schema Registry and Backward Compatibility
scenario_context: A team publishes Avro-encoded events to a message broker. They use a schema registry with BACKWARD compatibility mode enforced. A developer wants to rename the `user_id` field to `customer_id` to match the new domain model.
description: The schema registry rejects the rename with a compatibility violation error. Why does this happen, and what is the safest way to make the field name change without breaking existing consumers?
options: Renaming a field removes the old name from the schema, which breaks existing consumers that still reference `user_id`; the safe path is to add `customer_id` as an alias or new optional field first, migrate consumers, then deprecate `user_id`
The schema registry is misconfigured; renaming a field in Avro is always backward-compatible because field names are cosmetic metadata
The correct fix is to switch the schema registry to FULL compatibility mode, which allows field renames without breaking consumers
Consumers should be updated first to use `customer_id`, then the schema can be pushed to the registry; this order of operations satisfies BACKWARD compatibility
explanation: BACKWARD compatibility means a consumer using the new schema can read data that was produced under the previous schema. When `user_id` is renamed to `customer_id`, a consumer deserializing with the new v2 schema looks for a field called `customer_id` — but old messages only contain `user_id`. The new reader cannot find the expected field, so BACKWARD compatibility is violated and the registry rejects the change. The safe migration is additive: add `customer_id` as a new optional field (keeping `user_id` in place), migrate all consumers to read `customer_id`, then remove `user_id` in a final breaking-change release with a version bump. Option B is wrong — field names are part of the schema contract in Avro, not cosmetic metadata. Option C is incorrect — FULL compatibility still prohibits field renames; it enforces both BACKWARD and FORWARD simultaneously, making it stricter, not looser. Option D reverses the correct deployment order and does not address the schema structure problem — updating consumers before the new field exists in the schema still leaves old messages unreadable.
hints: Think about which direction BACKWARD compatibility protects: the reader using the new schema, or the reader using the old schema?
A safe migration strategy adds new structure first, shifts consumers, then removes the old structure — never the other way around.

title: Forward vs Backward Compatibility Trade-offs
description: A team has agreed that FORWARD compatibility is the contract for their event schema, but the schema registry is running in NONE mode — no automatic enforcement. A new producer adds a required field `payment_method` with no default value. Old consumers receive events containing this new field. What happens?
options: Old consumers that don't know about `payment_method` may fail or discard the field — forward compatibility requires that new fields are optional with defaults so old readers can safely ignore them
Forward compatibility guarantees old consumers handle any new fields transparently, so no consumer changes are needed
The producer's schema would be rejected by the registry because adding required fields always violates forward compatibility
Old consumers will automatically deserialize `payment_method` as NULL, preserving all other fields without errors
explanation: Forward compatibility means old schema readers (consumers) can read data written under the NEW schema. For that to hold, new fields must be optional or carry defaults — giving old consumers a safe fallback when they encounter an unknown field. When `payment_method` is added as required with no default, old consumers have no fallback and may crash or silently drop the field, violating the forward contract. Because the registry is in NONE mode, there is no registration-time gate: the violation is not caught until consumers receive real events at runtime. Option B overstates the guarantee — forward compat protects old readers only when new fields are optional with defaults, not unconditionally. Option C describes registry-enforcement behaviour, which is absent here (NONE mode means the registry accepts any schema change without validation). Option D assumes automatic NULL coercion, which depends on the serialization framework and is not guaranteed.
hints: Think about which side 'forward' protects: is it old readers consuming new data, or new readers consuming old data? That direction tells you what the constraint must be.
A required field with no default gives old consumers no fallback value — they have nothing to substitute when they encounter a field they don't recognise.

title: Data Contracts and Upstream Changes
scenario_context: A data engineering team maintains a transformation pipeline that reads from a source table owned by the application team. Without notice, the application team renames a column and changes a data type. The transformation pipeline begins failing silently, producing NULL values in several downstream reports.
description: The data engineering team wants to prevent this class of failure in the future. Which combination of practices provides the strongest protection?
options: Establish a data contract between producer and consumer specifying the schema, nullable constraints, and SLA; add automated schema validation tests that run on every pipeline trigger and alert on drift
Ask the application team to announce changes in a shared Slack channel at least one week in advance before modifying source tables
Add a schema cache to the pipeline so it uses the last-known-good schema and ignores upstream changes until a manual refresh is triggered
Switch to schema-on-read so the pipeline accepts any upstream format and applies transformations dynamically at query time
explanation: A data contract is a formal, machine-readable agreement between the producer (application team) and consumer (data engineering team) that specifies schema, types, nullability, and SLA. Combined with automated validation tests on every run, any drift is caught immediately with clear error messages rather than silently producing NULLs. Option B (Slack announcement) is informal and doesn't prevent the failure. Option C (schema cache) masks problems and delays discovery. Option D (schema-on-read) doesn't prevent silent failures — NULL values would still propagate if a column is renamed.
hints: Think about what mechanism makes the agreement between teams explicit and machine-enforceable rather than relying on human communication.
Detecting a contract violation at pipeline trigger time stops bad data immediately; detecting it at dashboard review time means damage has already propagated.

title: Micro-Batch vs True Streaming Latency
description: A team is building a real-time recommendation system. Events must be processed within 500 milliseconds of arriving to update user affinity scores. They are deciding between micro-batch (10-second trigger intervals) and native event-by-event streaming. Which should they choose, and why?
options: Native event-by-event streaming — micro-batch with 10-second intervals introduces at least 10 seconds of latency, violating the 500ms SLA
Micro-batch — it delivers lower latency than native streaming because small batches can be processed more efficiently with vectorized operations
Either approach works because both can meet sub-second SLAs when the cluster has enough compute capacity
Micro-batch — native streaming has higher operational overhead and should only be used when latency requirements are below 100 milliseconds
explanation: A 10-second micro-batch interval means an event arriving at t=0 is not processed until t=10s at the earliest — far beyond the 500ms SLA. Native streaming processes each event (or very small windows) as it arrives, achieving sub-second latency. Option B is wrong: micro-batch latency is bounded below by the trigger interval. Option C is incorrect — micro-batch latency is structurally bounded by the interval, not by compute. Option D reverses the trade-off: native streaming is used precisely for sub-second requirements.
hints: Consider the minimum possible latency for a micro-batch system: an event arriving just after a batch trigger must wait for the next trigger interval to elapse.
The trigger interval sets a hard lower bound on latency — no amount of additional compute can shrink latency below the batch window size.

title: Stateful Streaming: Session Windows
description: A streaming pipeline computes user session windows that close after 30 minutes of inactivity. An e-commerce user adds items to their cart, then goes idle for 45 minutes, then checks out. How many sessions does this create, and why?
options: Two sessions — the 30-minute inactivity gap exceeds the session timeout, so the cart-addition events form one session and the checkout event forms a new session
One session — the checkout event falls within the same calendar hour as the cart events, so they are grouped together
One session — streaming frameworks extend the session window whenever a new event arrives from the same user, regardless of gap
Three sessions — each distinct event type (add-to-cart, idle, checkout) constitutes its own session in an inactivity-based window
explanation: Session windows group events separated by less than the gap duration (here, 30 minutes). The 45-minute idle period exceeds the 30-minute timeout, so the window closes after the last cart event. The checkout event 45 minutes later opens a new session. Option B is wrong — session windows are defined by inactivity, not calendar time. Option C is wrong — session windows explicitly close after the gap threshold is exceeded; a new event reopens a new session. Option D is wrong — idle periods between events don't create their own sessions.
hints: Think about what 'inactivity gap' means as a closing condition for a session: what happens to the current session when no events arrive for longer than the gap?
Session windows are event-driven: a gap longer than the timeout closes the current window; the next event starts a fresh window.

title: Lambda Architecture Trade-offs
scenario_context: A team runs a Lambda architecture with a batch layer (overnight recomputation of all history) and a speed layer (real-time streaming for recent data). Business users query a serving layer that merges both. The team is spending significant engineering effort maintaining two separate codebases that must produce identical results.
description: A senior engineer proposes migrating to a Kappa architecture. Which statement accurately describes the trade-off the team should consider?
options: Kappa eliminates the batch layer by replaying events through the streaming system for both real-time and historical computation, reducing codebase duplication at the cost of requiring the streaming system to handle full historical replay efficiently
Kappa replaces the speed layer with a batch layer that runs every 5 minutes, achieving the same latency with simpler infrastructure
Kappa is identical to Lambda but with automated code synchronization between the batch and streaming codebases
Kappa eliminates the serving layer by pushing results directly to application databases, simplifying the query path
explanation: Kappa architecture removes the separate batch layer entirely. A single streaming system processes live data and can replay historical events from a log (like a message broker with long retention) to recompute history. This eliminates the dual-codebase maintenance problem but requires the streaming system to be capable of high-throughput historical replay — which can be expensive and operationally complex. Option B describes a different micro-batch hybrid, not Kappa. Option C is incorrect — Kappa merges the codebases, not synchronizes them. Option D is incorrect about Kappa's architectural changes.
hints: Think about what the 'Lambda' in the name represents architecturally (two paths) and what 'Kappa' does to that two-path structure.
The key question is whether your streaming system can serve as both the real-time and historical processing engine simultaneously.

title: Watermark Choice and State Store Size
scenario_context: A streaming pipeline processes clickstream events and computes 5-minute session counts. Event timestamps can arrive late due to mobile network delays. The current watermark is set to 2 minutes.
description: The team is seeing incomplete session counts because events regularly arrive 8–10 minutes late. They want to capture 95% of late events without unbounded state growth. What should they change?
options: Increase the watermark to 15 minutes to safely cover the 95th-percentile lateness while accepting higher state store memory usage
Decrease the watermark to 30 seconds to reduce state store size and rely on downstream correction jobs
Switch from event time to processing time so late arrivals are always included in the current window
Disable watermarking entirely so all late events are always included regardless of arrival time
explanation: The watermark defines how long the engine retains state for a window after the window's end time. Increasing it to 15 minutes captures late events up to 15 minutes after the window closes, covering the observed 95th-percentile delay. The trade-off is higher state store memory. Option B makes lateness worse. Option C is wrong — processing time ignores event time entirely, losing session semantics. Option D would cause unbounded state growth, which is operationally unsustainable.
hints: Consider what determines how long a streaming engine keeps state for a window open after its theoretical close time.
A longer allowed delay means more state is retained in memory; the right setting balances coverage against resource use.

title: Event Time vs Processing Time
description: A mobile app batches events locally and uploads them when connectivity is restored — sometimes hours later. A streaming job uses processing time for its hourly aggregation windows. What problem does this create?
options: Events that occurred at 2 PM are processed at 8 PM and assigned to the 8 PM window, making the 2 PM window incomplete and the 8 PM window inflated
Processing time windows are always accurate because they reflect when computation actually occurred, which is the correct semantic for mobile apps
Event time would cause the same problem because the pipeline cannot know when events were originally generated
The pipeline should use ingestion time, which automatically corrects for mobile upload delays by snapping events to the batch upload timestamp
explanation: Processing time uses the wall-clock time when the event arrives at the processing engine. A 2 PM event uploaded at 8 PM is stamped at 8 PM, corrupting both windows. Event time uses the timestamp embedded in the event (when it was generated on the device), allowing correct assignment to the 2 PM window with appropriate watermarking for late arrivals. Option B is wrong — processing time is incorrect for this use case. Option C is wrong — event time specifically solves this problem. Option D is wrong — ingestion time stamps events at arrival, not generation, causing the same problem.
hints: Think about the three timestamps in a streaming system: when the event occurred, when it arrived at the broker, and when the processor received it — which one reflects the user's actual activity?
For mobile devices with intermittent connectivity, the time stamped on the device is the only reliable indicator of when the event actually happened.

title: Watermark and Window Completeness
description: A streaming job uses a 10-minute tumbling window with a 5-minute watermark. An event with event_time = 10:05 AM arrives at processing_time = 10:22 AM. The watermark at 10:22 AM is at 10:17 AM. Is the event included in the 10:00–10:10 window?
options: No — the watermark at 10:17 AM has already passed the window's end time (10:10 AM), so the 10:00–10:10 window is already closed and the event is dropped as late
Yes — the event's event_time (10:05 AM) falls within the 10:00–10:10 window, so it is always included regardless of watermark
Yes — the watermark only closes windows after it exceeds the window end by more than the watermark delay (5 minutes), so the window is still open until 10:22 AM
No — the event arrived after 10:10 AM processing time, which is all that matters for window assignment
explanation: A window closes when the watermark advances past the window's end time. The 10:00–10:10 window closes when the watermark reaches 10:10 AM. With a 5-minute watermark, the engine waits until processing_time ~10:15 AM to advance the watermark past 10:10 AM. By 10:22 AM, the watermark is at 10:17 AM, which is past the window's end (10:10 AM), so the window has already closed. The late-arriving event is dropped. Option B ignores the watermark mechanism. Option C misreads the watermark semantics. Option D is wrong — event time, not processing time, determines window assignment.
hints: Consider when the 10:00–10:10 window closes: the engine must be confident no more events in that range can arrive. What determines that confidence level?
Once the allowed latency threshold has been exceeded for a window's end time, that window's result is emitted and state is discarded — events arriving after that point are dropped.

title: Data Quality: Schema Drift Detection
scenario_context: A data pipeline ingests JSON events from a third-party API. The API occasionally adds new fields, changes field types, or removes optional fields without announcing changes. Downstream transformations break silently when field types change from string to integer.
description: Which data quality strategy best addresses silent schema drift from an external API?
options: Implement automated schema inference on each ingestion run and compare against a stored baseline schema; alert and halt on type changes while allowing new optional fields to pass through with logging
Validate only the required fields on each run and ignore all other fields; type changes in optional fields will not break required-field logic
Store raw JSON as-is without any schema validation; apply type casting in the transformation layer where errors can be caught per-field
Request the API provider to implement a schema registry; until then, accept all changes and fix downstream queries manually when they break
explanation: Automated schema comparison (stored baseline vs. inferred schema at ingest time) catches both type changes and removals immediately, before they propagate to transformations. Alerting on type changes and halting prevents silent corruption. Allowing new optional fields with logging balances strictness with forward compatibility. Option B is insufficient — type changes in optional fields can propagate silently and cause subtle errors downstream. Option C defers type errors to transformations, where they produce silent NULLs or cast failures that are harder to diagnose. Option D has no protective mechanism and relies on after-the-fact manual repair.
hints: Think about where in the pipeline you gain the most leverage: catching a type change at entry versus discovering its effects in a downstream report.
A stored reference schema gives you a concrete baseline to compare against; without it, you have no way to know what 'normal' looks like.

title: Data Quality: Row Count Assertions
description: A daily pipeline loads 1 million rows on average. One day it loads 12 rows. No errors were raised. Which assertion type would have caught this anomaly?
options: A row count threshold assertion that fails when the row count deviates by more than a configured percentage from a rolling 7-day average
A schema validation check that verifies all required columns are present and non-null in the loaded rows
A uniqueness constraint on the primary key that prevents duplicate rows from being inserted
A foreign key constraint that ensures each loaded row references a valid entry in a parent dimension table
explanation: A row count anomaly check compares today's loaded count against historical baselines (e.g., rolling average) and raises an alert when the deviation is statistically abnormal. Loading 12 rows instead of ~1 million is a 99.999% drop — a clear anomaly. Schema validation (Option B) only checks column structure, not row volume. Uniqueness constraints (Option C) prevent duplicates but don't detect volume drops. Foreign key checks (Option D) validate referential integrity, not completeness of the loaded batch.
hints: Think about what category of data quality check monitors volume rather than individual row structure.
A sudden drop from millions of rows to a handful is a completeness signal — the pipeline didn't fail, but the data is almost entirely missing.

title: Exactly-Once Semantics: Producer Side
description: A producer sends a message to a message broker. The broker receives and writes the message, but the acknowledgment is lost in the network. The producer retries. With at-least-once semantics, a duplicate exists in the broker. What mechanism do transactional producers use to achieve exactly-once semantics in this scenario?
options: Producers assign a sequence number to each message; the broker detects and deduplicates retries by comparing sequence numbers to the last committed offset per producer
Producers wait for two acknowledgments (from the leader and one replica) before considering the message committed, preventing retry-induced duplicates
Producers use a two-phase commit with the broker: the message is written tentatively, and only committed after the producer confirms receipt of the ack
Producers disable retries entirely so no duplicates can be created; messages that fail are logged for manual resubmission
explanation: Idempotent producers assign a monotonically increasing sequence number to each message. If the broker receives a retry with the same sequence number from the same producer session, it recognizes it as a duplicate and discards it without writing again. This makes producer-side exactly-once possible. Option B (waiting for replica acks) improves durability but does not prevent duplicates on retry. Option C describes a two-phase commit, which is a different coordination mechanism. Option D sacrifices reliability entirely.
hints: Think about what unique identifier a producer could attach to each send attempt that would allow the broker to recognize a repeated attempt.
If the broker can tell 'I already saw this message from this producer session,' it can safely discard the retry without writing a duplicate.

title: End-to-End Exactly-Once in a Pipeline
scenario_context: A payment processing pipeline reads from a message broker, transforms the events, and writes results to a database. The team uses a streaming framework with end-to-end exactly-once guarantees enabled.
description: The pipeline crashes mid-processing and restarts from a checkpoint. Which combination of properties makes the end-to-end exactly-once guarantee hold?
options: The framework checkpoints consumer offsets and output state atomically; on restart, it re-reads from the last committed offset and overwrites any partial output written before the crash, ensuring each message's effect appears exactly once
The framework resends all messages in the window from the beginning of the stream, then deduplicates the output table using the primary key before final commit
The framework discards all state after a crash and reprocesses only the messages that arrived after the restart, accepting loss of in-flight messages as a trade-off for consistency
The framework marks crashed messages as dead letters and processes them separately to avoid double-counting in the main pipeline
explanation: End-to-end exactly-once requires atomic checkpointing: both the input offset (how far the consumer has read) and the output state (what has been written to the sink) are committed together. On restart, the system re-reads from the last checkpoint and uses idempotent writes (or transactional sinks) to ensure the output reflects each message exactly once. Option B achieves exactly-once for the output but is expensive and not how frameworks implement it internally. Option C describes at-most-once. Option D describes dead-letter handling, which does not provide exactly-once for the main path.
hints: Think about what 'atomic checkpoint' means in this context: what two things must be checkpointed together for the guarantee to hold?
If the checkpoint records where reading stopped and what was written, a restart can recover to exactly that state without redoing or losing any work.

title: Orchestration: Fan-Out Task Design
scenario_context: A data pipeline processes 50 regional sales files every morning. Currently, a single sequential task downloads and processes each file one by one. The pipeline takes 4 hours. Business users need results by 6 AM but the pipeline starts at 2 AM.
description: Which orchestration pattern reduces wall-clock time most effectively for this workload?
options: Fan-out parallelism: spawn 50 parallel tasks (one per file), each completing independently, then a single fan-in task aggregates results — reduces wall-clock time to roughly the duration of the slowest single file plus aggregation
Chunked batching: group files into 5 batches of 10 and process each batch sequentially, reducing time by 5x compared to individual sequential processing
Dynamic task mapping with a global lock: process all 50 files concurrently but acquire a database lock before each write to prevent conflicts
Increase the compute resources of the single sequential task until it runs fast enough to meet the 6 AM deadline
explanation: Fan-out parallelism is the correct pattern: each file is an independent unit of work with no cross-file dependencies, making true parallel execution possible. The total wall-clock time becomes approximately max(individual file times) + aggregation time, rather than sum(all file times). This is the maximum possible speedup. Option B (batching into groups of 10) still processes sequentially within each group and reduces time by at most 10x, not the full 50x. Option C introduces a global lock that serializes the most expensive step (writing), negating the parallelism benefit. Option D (vertical scaling) has physical limits and cannot match the 50x parallelism gain.
hints: Think about the relationship between the files: do they share state, depend on each other, or can each be processed in complete isolation?
When tasks are fully independent, parallel execution shrinks wall-clock time toward the duration of the single slowest task — very different from sequential sum.

title: Orchestration: Event-Driven vs Schedule Trigger
description: A downstream pipeline must run only after an upstream team's pipeline completes and drops a completion marker file. The upstream team's completion time varies between 30 minutes and 3 hours. What orchestration trigger is most appropriate?
options: An event-driven file-presence check that polls for the marker file and triggers the downstream pipeline immediately when it appears
A fixed schedule trigger set to 4 hours after the expected start, guaranteeing the upstream is complete before the downstream begins
A manual trigger requiring an upstream team member to click a button in the orchestration UI after their pipeline finishes
A time-based dependency with a 95th-percentile buffer: schedule the downstream to start 3.5 hours after the upstream's typical start time
explanation: An event-driven trigger (file sensor or equivalent) responds to the actual state change — the marker file appearing — and starts the downstream pipeline immediately. This minimizes latency regardless of whether the upstream finishes in 30 minutes or 3 hours. Option B (fixed 4-hour delay) wastes time when upstream finishes early and fails when upstream takes longer than expected. Option C (manual trigger) is error-prone and creates human bottlenecks. Option D (95th-percentile buffer) is better than fixed scheduling but still wastes time when upstream is fast and fails on the rare slow run.
hints: Think about the core problem with time-based triggers when the dependency duration is variable: what happens when upstream finishes 2.5 hours before the scheduled trigger?
An event-driven trigger acts the moment its condition is true, not at a predetermined time — this directly solves the variable-duration problem.

title: SLA Breach: Root Cause vs Symptom
scenario_context: A daily pipeline that produces the revenue report has an SLA of 7 AM. Over the past two weeks, the pipeline has breached its SLA on 6 out of 14 days. The pipeline starts at 5 AM. Investigation shows that on breach days, a JOIN between two tables takes 45 minutes instead of the usual 10 minutes.
description: The SLA breach is a symptom. Which root cause analysis approach correctly identifies what to investigate?
options: Profile the JOIN operation on breach days vs normal days — look for data volume spikes, skewed key distribution, or missing statistics that cause a suboptimal query plan
Move the pipeline start time from 5 AM to 3 AM to add a 2-hour buffer before the 7 AM SLA
Increase the number of parallel workers for the JOIN step to 10x to ensure it always completes within the time budget
Switch the SLA from 7 AM to 9 AM to reflect the realistic p95 completion time and avoid frequent breaches
explanation: The symptom is the SLA breach; the root cause is the 4-5x JOIN slowdown on specific days. Profiling the JOIN on breach days vs normal days is the correct diagnostic approach: data volume spikes (e.g., end-of-month batch loads), key skew, or stale query planner statistics are common causes of dramatic and intermittent slowdowns. Option B (earlier start) masks the problem without fixing it. Option C (more workers) may help for some causes but is a guess without diagnosis. Option D (change the SLA) avoids fixing the underlying problem.
hints: The key signal is that the slowdown is intermittent — it happens on some days and not others. What about those specific days might be different?
The answer lies in understanding what changed between fast days and slow days: volume, distribution of keys, or available statistics.

title: SLA Budgeting Across Pipeline Stages
description: A pipeline has an end-to-end SLA of 60 minutes. It has three sequential stages: ingestion (10 min), transformation (35 min), and serving (10 min). The total is 55 minutes, giving only a 5-minute SLA buffer. How should the team improve resilience against occasional stage overruns?
options: Set stage-level SLOs (e.g., ingestion ≤12 min, transformation ≤38 min, serving ≤10 min) with automated alerts when any stage exceeds its budget, enabling early intervention before end-to-end SLA is breached
Add a 15-minute sleep step between ingestion and transformation to create a buffer for slow ingestion days
Reduce the end-to-end SLA from 60 minutes to 45 minutes to force the team to optimize each stage
Merge the three stages into a single monolithic job so the scheduler overhead between stages is eliminated
explanation: Stage-level SLOs give the team early warning: if transformation hits 42 minutes (over its 38-minute budget), the alert fires while there's still time to intervene or scale resources before the 60-minute SLA is breached. This is proactive SLA management. Option B (sleep step) wastes time and reduces the actual buffer. Option C (tighten the SLA) creates pressure but doesn't add operational resilience. Option D (monolithic job) removes stage isolation, making debugging harder and providing no early warning capability.
hints: Think about what operational tool gives you advance notice that the end-to-end SLA is at risk, before it actually breaches.
Stage-level targets that sum to less than the total SLA create a buffer — when a stage exceeds its budget, you know you're on track to miss the SLA.

title: Backfill Design: Partition-Aware Reruns
description: A daily pipeline failed for 5 days due to a bug that has now been fixed. The pipeline must reprocess the 5 missing days. Which backfill strategy is most operationally safe?
options: Run one day at a time in chronological order, validating each partition's output before triggering the next, to catch any residual issues early without contaminating multiple days at once
Run all 5 days in parallel simultaneously to recover as fast as possible and minimize the total wall-clock recovery time
Reprocess only the most recent day and use it to extrapolate the missing values for the other 4 days
Skip the backfill and process only from today forward, accepting the 5-day gap as historical data loss
explanation: Sequential, validated backfills are safer than parallel execution, especially after a bug fix. Running one day at a time allows the team to verify each partition is correct before proceeding — if the fix was incomplete or there are edge cases, the damage is limited to one partition rather than all five simultaneously. Option B (parallel) is faster but risks compounding errors across all 5 days simultaneously. Option C (extrapolation) is not appropriate for factual historical data. Option D (skip) is only acceptable if the data has no business value.
hints: Think about what happens if the fix is incomplete and you ran all 5 days in parallel — how do you recover if the output is wrong for all of them?
A sequential approach with validation gates limits the blast radius: a problem in day 2 is caught before days 3–5 are processed.

title: Backfill Design: Making Jobs Backfill-Safe
scenario_context: A pipeline writes daily aggregates to a target table by appending rows. The job uses the execution date as the `report_date` column. When a backfill is triggered for a historical date, the job appends new rows alongside the original (now-stale) rows from the first run.
description: Which design change makes this pipeline safe to backfill without creating duplicate report dates?
options: Use a DELETE-then-INSERT or MERGE pattern keyed on `report_date` so each backfill run atomically replaces any existing rows for that date
Add a `run_timestamp` column so consumers can filter to the latest run per `report_date` using a MAX() query
Switch from a `report_date` partition key to an auto-increment row ID so each backfill creates distinct rows that don't conflict
Require manual deletion of existing `report_date` rows before triggering a backfill to ensure clean state
explanation: A DELETE-then-INSERT or MERGE (UPSERT) keyed on `report_date` makes the job idempotent: running it for the same date multiple times always produces the same final state — one set of correct rows for that date. Option B (run_timestamp filtering) works for consumers but doesn't fix the underlying data model — stale rows accumulate and queries become more complex. Option C removes the semantic key, making the data harder to query. Option D (manual cleanup) is error-prone and doesn't scale for large backfills.
hints: Think about what operation would guarantee that after running the job for a specific date, exactly one version of that date's data exists in the table.
The pattern that achieves this replaces existing data for a partition rather than adding to it.

title: Partition Pruning: Filter Pushdown
description: A table is partitioned by `region` and `event_date`. A query filters `WHERE region = 'US' AND event_date >= '2024-01-01'`. Which statement about predicate pushdown is correct?
options: The query engine pushes both predicates down to the storage layer, skipping all partitions that don't match either condition before reading any data
Predicate pushdown only works for equality filters; the range filter on `event_date` must be applied after reading all regional partitions
Partitioning on two columns disables predicate pushdown because the engine cannot evaluate composite partition keys efficiently
Predicate pushdown applies only to the first partition column; the engine must read all `region = 'US'` partitions regardless of `event_date`
explanation: Columnar and partitioned storage formats (Parquet, ORC, Iceberg) support predicate pushdown for both equality and range filters. The query engine evaluates both conditions against partition metadata, skipping partitions where `region != 'US'` OR `event_date < '2024-01-01'`. Both predicates are applied before any data is read. Option B is incorrect — range filters are commonly supported for predicate pushdown. Option C is incorrect — composite partition keys work efficiently. Option D is incorrect — modern engines apply pushdown to all partition columns.
hints: Think about what 'pushdown' means: the filter logic moves closer to the storage layer rather than being applied after data is loaded into memory.
Modern table formats store partition metadata separately from data files, allowing the engine to evaluate filters without opening any data files.

title: Data Skew in Partitioned Joins
scenario_context: A distributed join processes orders partitioned by `customer_id`. The top 0.1% of customers (enterprise accounts) generate 60% of all orders. During the join, a few worker nodes are overloaded while most are idle.
description: This is a data skew problem. Which technique most effectively addresses it?
options: Salting the skewed keys: append a random integer suffix (e.g., 0–9) to enterprise customer IDs before partitioning, then aggregate the salted partitions in a second step — this distributes the hot key's data across multiple workers
Repartition the orders table by `order_date` instead of `customer_id` before the join to avoid skewed key distribution
Filter out enterprise customers before the join and process them in a separate sequential pipeline to prevent overloading the distributed workers
Increase the memory allocation for the overloaded worker nodes so they can handle the disproportionate data volume
explanation: Salting distributes hot keys across multiple partitions by making each 'copy' of a hot key (e.g., enterprise_id + random suffix) land on a different worker. After the join, the partial results are aggregated to reconstruct the full result. This uses all workers for hot-key processing. Option B (repartition by date) may still produce skew if certain dates have many enterprise orders. Option C (separate sequential processing) works but doesn't scale. Option D (more memory) is vertical scaling and has limits; it doesn't fix the underlying distribution problem.
hints: Think about why a hot key causes skew: all rows with that key land on the same partition. What transformation would spread those rows across multiple partitions?
By making the key artificially non-unique before partitioning and then reassembling the result afterward, you exploit the full cluster capacity.

title: Parquet vs Avro: Choosing a File Format
description: A team needs to choose a file format for a data lakehouse. Two use cases exist: (1) high-throughput analytics with aggregations over a few columns from wide tables, and (2) event streaming where each full record must be serialized and deserialized efficiently. Which format pair is most appropriate?
options: Parquet for analytics (columnar layout enables column-level I/O skipping) and Avro for streaming (row-oriented serialization is fast for full-record processing)
Avro for both use cases because it supports schema evolution and handles both streaming and analytics equally well
Parquet for both use cases because its compression ratios are always superior to Avro for any access pattern
CSV for analytics (human-readable and universally compatible) and Parquet for streaming (better compression than Avro)
explanation: Parquet is columnar: analytics queries that read 2–3 columns from a 100-column table read only those columns' byte ranges, skipping the rest. Avro is row-oriented: each record is stored together, making full-record serialization (as needed in streaming producers/consumers) fast and compact. Using each format where it excels is the correct choice. Option B is wrong — Avro is a poor choice for columnar analytics. Option C is wrong — Parquet's columnar layout is inefficient for full-record streaming access. Option D is wrong — CSV is never suitable for high-throughput analytics.
hints: Think about the access pattern for each use case: analytics reads a few columns across many rows; streaming reads all columns of individual records.
The physical storage layout determines I/O efficiency: adjacent columns benefit aggregate queries; adjacent rows benefit record-at-a-time processing.

title: Compaction: Solving the Small File Problem
scenario_context: A streaming pipeline writes Parquet files to a data lake every 30 seconds, producing 2,880 files per day for a single table partition. After one month, the partition contains 86,400 tiny files. Queries on this table have degraded from 10 seconds to 4 minutes.
description: The team wants to fix query performance without changing the streaming ingestion frequency. What is the correct approach?
options: Schedule a periodic compaction job that merges small files into larger target sizes (e.g., 128–512 MB each), reducing file count while preserving data — run compaction asynchronously so streaming ingestion is not blocked
Increase the streaming trigger interval to 1 hour to produce fewer, larger files and avoid the small-file problem entirely
Enable delta compression in the streaming framework so each new file stores only the difference from the previous file, reducing file count
Switch from Parquet to CSV for the data lake table, which handles many small files more efficiently due to its simpler format
explanation: Compaction is the standard solution: a background job reads many small files and rewrites them as fewer large files without changing the data. This restores sequential read performance and reduces file system metadata overhead. Modern table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake) support transactional compaction that doesn't interrupt live queries. Option B (increasing streaming interval) changes the ingestion SLA, which may be unacceptable. Option C (delta compression) is a different concept and doesn't reduce file count. Option D is wrong — CSV has no advantage for many small files.
hints: Think about the two ways to reduce file count: change how data is written (affects ingestion) or periodically merge existing files (affects only storage).
An asynchronous merge operation that doesn't affect the ingestion path satisfies both the streaming frequency requirement and the query performance requirement.

title: CDC: Handling DDL Changes
description: A log-based CDC pipeline is replicating a source table to a data warehouse. The source DBA adds a new NOT NULL column with a default value. What must the CDC pipeline do to handle this change correctly?
options: Detect the DDL change event in the transaction log, apply the schema change to the target table, and ensure subsequent DML events include the new column's value
Restart the CDC pipeline from the beginning of the log to reprocess all historical events with the new schema applied
Pause ingestion until the target table is manually altered by the warehouse DBA, then resume the pipeline
Drop and recreate the target table with the new schema, then restart a full initial load from the source
explanation: Production-grade CDC tools capture DDL events (ALTER TABLE) from the transaction log alongside DML events. When a schema change is detected, the tool propagates the ALTER to the target and continues streaming. For a NOT NULL column with a default, historical rows receive the default value, while new events include the actual column value. Option B (restart from beginning) is expensive and unnecessary. Option C (manual pause) is operationally fragile. Option D (drop and recreate) is the most disruptive option and causes full data unavailability.
hints: Think about what types of events a CDC tool reads from a transaction log — it's not only row-level changes; structural changes are also logged.
A good CDC system handles schema changes as first-class events, propagating them to the target automatically.

title: CDC: Initial Load Sequencing
description: A team sets up CDC on a production database table with 500 million existing rows. They need to get all current data into the warehouse first, then switch to capturing incremental changes. What is the correct sequencing?
options: Record the current log offset before the initial full load begins; after the full load completes, replay CDC events from that offset to catch changes that occurred during the load
Complete the full initial load, then enable CDC — any changes that occurred during the load will be picked up by the first CDC run using a timestamp filter
Enable CDC first, wait for it to catch up to the current log position, then perform the initial load from a database snapshot
Perform the initial load and CDC ingestion simultaneously; use a deduplication step to merge overlapping records
explanation: The correct sequence is: (1) record the current log position (offset/LSN), (2) perform the full snapshot load while the source continues to change, (3) after the snapshot completes, replay CDC events from the saved offset forward. This ensures no changes are lost during the (potentially hours-long) snapshot load. Option B is incorrect — enabling CDC after the load means changes during the load are lost. Option C is impractical — the log grows continuously. Option D creates unresolvable conflicts between snapshot and CDC data for rows modified during the load.
hints: Think about what happens to the transaction log during a multi-hour full load: the log keeps growing. How do you ensure you capture changes that occurred while the load was running?
The key insight is that you must record your position in the log before the snapshot, so you know where to start replaying after the snapshot completes.

title: Data Lineage: Column-Level Tracking
description: A compliance team asks: 'Which source columns contribute to the `revenue_usd` column in the executive dashboard?' This requires tracing data through 12 transformation steps. What type of lineage is needed?
options: Column-level lineage — tracks how each individual output column is derived from specific source columns through transformations
Table-level lineage — identifies which source tables contribute to the dashboard table without tracking individual column origins
Row-level lineage — traces each individual row back to its source record in the origin table
Job-level lineage — records which pipeline jobs wrote to the dashboard table and when
explanation: Column-level lineage (also called field-level lineage) traces the derivation of each output column through all intermediate transformations back to its source columns. For compliance, knowing which tables fed the dashboard (table-level) is insufficient; you need to know exactly which source fields were used and how they were combined to produce `revenue_usd`. Table-level lineage (Option B) is too coarse. Row-level lineage (Option C) is for auditing specific records, not column derivation. Job-level lineage (Option D) only shows when jobs ran.
hints: Think about the granularity of the question: the compliance team wants to know about one specific column's origins, not about the table as a whole.
Transformations like SUM(price * quantity) derive a column from two source columns — tracking that derivation at the field level answers the compliance question.

title: Observability: Freshness Monitoring
scenario_context: A data team maintains 40 pipelines feeding 200 downstream tables. Last month, three SLA breaches went undetected for over 6 hours because no one noticed the dashboard was stale. The team has no centralized monitoring for pipeline completion or data freshness.
description: Which observability setup provides the strongest early warning for future SLA breaches?
options: Implement table-level freshness monitoring that checks the MAX(updated_at) timestamp against expected SLA thresholds, and send alerts when a table hasn't been updated within its expected window — integrate with an on-call rotation for SLA-critical tables
Add logging to each pipeline that prints 'Pipeline complete' to stdout, then manually grep logs when users report stale data
Require all pipeline owners to send a Slack message when their pipeline completes, and create a shared checklist for the on-call team to verify
Build a custom web dashboard that displays the last-run time for each pipeline; have the on-call team check it every 30 minutes
explanation: Automated freshness monitoring with threshold-based alerting is the only solution that provides early, automatic detection without human polling. Checking MAX(updated_at) per table against SLA windows catches freshness violations immediately after they occur and routes alerts to the on-call team. Options B, C, and D all require human intervention to detect the problem — they are reactive, not proactive, and require someone to already suspect a problem before looking.
hints: Think about whether the detection mechanism requires a human to initiate a check, or whether it fires automatically when a threshold is exceeded.
Six-hour detection gaps happen when monitoring is polling-based and human-initiated; automated threshold alerting closes that gap to minutes.

title: Cost Optimization: Format and Partition Impact
description: A data team spends 70% of their cloud budget on query compute. Most queries filter on `event_date` and aggregate `revenue`. The table stores 3 years of history with 500 billion rows in CSV format. Which change has the largest cost-reduction impact?
options: Convert to columnar Parquet with Snappy compression and partition by `event_date` — this combines column pruning, compression, and partition pruning to reduce bytes scanned by 90%+
Move the table to cold storage (e.g., archive tier) to reduce storage costs, and restore it on demand when queries are needed
Add a materialized view with pre-aggregated daily totals so analysts query the summary rather than raw data
Increase the warehouse's concurrency capacity so more queries run in parallel, reducing per-query wait time and overall cost
explanation: Converting from CSV to columnar Parquet with date partitioning attacks compute cost at the root: (1) partitioning by `event_date` prunes irrelevant date ranges before any data is read; (2) columnar format reads only `event_date` and `revenue`, skipping all other columns; (3) Snappy compression reduces bytes transferred. Together, these can reduce scanned bytes by 90%+ for typical analytics queries, directly cutting compute costs. Option B reduces storage cost, not compute. Option C (materialized view) helps for specific pre-defined aggregations but doesn't help ad-hoc queries. Option D (more concurrency) increases cost, not reduces it.
hints: Cloud compute costs are proportional to bytes scanned. What storage format and organization reduce the bytes a query must read for a date-filtered, two-column aggregation?
Three levers reduce scan cost simultaneously: avoid reading unnecessary rows (partitioning), avoid reading unnecessary columns (columnar), and shrink the physical file size (compression).

title: Cost Optimization: Tiered Storage
scenario_context: A company stores 5 years of clickstream data in a high-performance lakehouse. Storage costs are $50,000/month. Analysis shows that 95% of queries access data from the last 90 days; data older than 1 year is queried fewer than 5 times per month.
description: Which storage tiering strategy reduces cost while maintaining acceptable query performance for the access patterns described?
options: Keep the last 90 days in hot storage, move 90 days–1 year data to warm (infrequent access) storage, and archive data older than 1 year to cold storage — accept higher latency for rare historical queries
Delete all data older than 90 days to eliminate the cost of storing rarely accessed historical data
Move all 5 years of data to cold archive storage and restore on demand, since the team can tolerate delays for any query
Keep the last year in hot storage for simplicity, even though 75% of it is rarely queried — the operational complexity of tiering is not worth the savings
explanation: Tiered storage aligns storage cost with access frequency: hot storage (fast, expensive) for frequently queried data; warm storage (cheaper, slightly slower) for moderately accessed data; cold/archive (cheapest, slowest restore) for rarely accessed historical data. The 90-day hot window covers 95% of queries at high performance. Data between 90 days and 1 year is occasionally queried and benefits from warm storage. Archives older than 1 year are so rarely accessed that cold storage latency is acceptable. Option B (delete data) destroys historical value. Option C (cold for everything) makes common queries unacceptably slow. Option D overspends significantly.
hints: Think about matching storage cost to query frequency: what fraction of queries would be affected by slower retrieval, and is that trade-off acceptable for each tier?
The majority of queries hit recent data — aligning the hot tier to cover those queries preserves performance where it matters and saves cost where it doesn't.

title: ELT Transformation Layers: Debugging a Wrong Metric
description: An ELT architecture has three layers: raw (verbatim source data), staging (cleaned, typed, deduplicated), and mart (business-logic aggregates). A data analyst reports that a revenue metric is wrong. What is the correct order to investigate?
options: Start at the mart layer to check business logic; if correct, inspect staging for data quality issues; trace to raw last if the problem isn't found upstream
Start at the raw layer to verify the source data arrived correctly, then check staging, then the mart
Check staging first because most data quality bugs are introduced during cleaning and type casting
Check all three layers simultaneously to save time, then triangulate where the discrepancy first appears
explanation: Debugging a wrong metric requires systematic backward tracing starting closest to where the symptom appears. The mart layer is where the metric is computed — if the formula and JOIN logic look correct, move to staging to check for data quality issues (nulls, type errors, deduplication failures), then to raw if staging also looks clean. This approach narrows the problem efficiently. Option B (start at raw) is inefficient; most logic errors live in the mart. Option C (start at staging) skips the most likely culprit (mart business logic). Option D (simultaneous) is impractical without clear signals and leads to confusion.
hints: Think about where business logic lives and where most logic errors are introduced — the layer closest to the output or the layer closest to the source?
A systematic debugging approach starts closest to where the symptom appears and works backward toward the source only if needed.

title: Backpressure in a Streaming Pipeline
scenario_context: A real-time enrichment pipeline reads from a Kafka topic (producer rate: 50,000 messages/sec), calls an external enrichment API per message, and writes to a second Kafka topic. Over the past hour the consumer lag has grown from 10K to 4.2M messages. Enrichment API latency is stable at 12ms per call. The consumer group has 8 pods, each processing messages sequentially.
description: What is the root cause of the growing lag, and what is the most effective first remediation step?
options: The consumer throughput (8 pods × 1 call/12ms ≈ 667 msg/sec) is far below the producer rate (50,000 msg/sec) — this is backpressure; the most effective fix is to increase consumer parallelism (more pods or async batched API calls) to raise throughput above the producer rate

The growing lag is caused by the Kafka topic having too few partitions — Kafka limits one consumer per partition, so adding more pods beyond the partition count has no effect; the fix is to increase the partition count to match the desired pod count
The enrichment API is the bottleneck because 12ms per call is too slow; the correct fix is to cache API responses in Redis so repeated lookups return in under 1ms and the consumer can catch up

The consumer lag is a monitoring artifact — Kafka resets consumer offsets when lag exceeds a threshold; the actual processing is healthy and the lag will self-correct once the consumer group rebalances
explanation:
Backpressure occurs when the consumer's processing throughput is lower than the producer's write rate, causing the queue (Kafka consumer lag) to grow unboundedly. Here: 8 pods × (1000ms / 12ms) ≈ 667 messages/sec capacity vs 50,000 messages/sec produced — a 75× gap. The primary fix is to increase parallelism: add more consumer pods (requires enough Kafka partitions to support them) and/or switch from sequential to async/batched API calls. With 50 concurrent async calls per pod at 12ms each, a single pod achieves ~4,100 msg/sec; 12 such pods ≈ 50,000 msg/sec.

Option B is partially correct as a prerequisite (partition count does cap parallelism) but it is the second step, not the root cause diagnosis. The root cause is the throughput math, not partition count alone.

Option C (caching) helps only if a large fraction of enrichment calls are repeated lookups for the same key. Nothing in the scenario indicates repeated keys — treating it as the primary fix is speculative.

Option D is false — Kafka consumer lag is a real metric and does not self-correct without intervention.
hints: Calculate the maximum throughput achievable with the current setup (pods × messages per second per pod) and compare it to the producer rate.
Backpressure means the consumer cannot keep up with the producer. The solution always involves increasing consumer throughput, reducing the work per message, or slowing the producer.

title: GDPR Erasure in an Immutable Data Lake: Crypto Shredding
description: A data platform stores Parquet files in S3 and uses Spark for batch processing. The legal team requires GDPR-compliant erasure within 72 hours of a deletion request, but the raw Parquet files are immutable and cannot be retroactively modified. Which approach satisfies the erasure requirement without physically rewriting historical Parquet files?
options: Crypto shredding: encrypt each user's PII fields with a per-user key stored in a KMS; on erasure request, delete the user's key from the KMS — the encrypted data in Parquet becomes permanently unreadable without rewriting any files

Pseudonymization: replace user PII with a deterministic hash at ingest time; on erasure request, delete the hash mapping from the lookup table — the hash in Parquet is irreversible without the mapping

Data masking: apply column-level masking policies in the query engine (e.g., Apache Ranger) so that deleted users' PII is replaced with NULL at read time — physical data is unchanged but logically erased
Partition-level deletion: partition Parquet files by user_id so each user's data lands in its own partition directory; on erasure request, delete the S3 prefix for that user
explanation:
Crypto shredding (cryptographic erasure) is the standard technique for GDPR erasure in immutable storage systems. Each user's sensitive columns are encrypted with a unique key managed in a KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, etc.). When a deletion request arrives, the key is deleted from the KMS. Without the key, the ciphertext in Parquet files is computationally indistinguishable from random data and cannot be decrypted — GDPR considers this equivalent to erasure. No Parquet files need to be rewritten.

Option B (pseudonymization) is not sufficient. GDPR considers pseudonymous data still personal if re-identification is possible. Deleting the mapping table removes the easy lookup path, but if the original data space is small enough to brute-force, the hash can be reversed.

Option C (query-layer masking) is access control, not erasure. The physical PII still exists in the Parquet files; it is merely hidden at read time. A user with direct S3 access could still read it. This does not satisfy GDPR's right to erasure.

Option D (partition-level deletion by user_id) physically deletes data but requires partitioning by user_id — impractical for analytical fact tables because it creates millions of tiny partitions and breaks date-range query efficiency.
hints: GDPR's right to erasure requires that data can no longer be accessed or reconstructed. What happens to encrypted data when its decryption key is destroyed?
Masking and pseudonymization hide data from readers but don't remove it from storage. Crypto shredding is different — why?

title: Operationalizing Data Contracts: Schema Registry and CI Enforcement
description: A data platform team wants to formalize data contracts between producer and consumer teams. Which mechanism most effectively prevents breaking schema changes from reaching downstream consumers in a continuous deployment environment?
options: Store schema definitions as versioned files in a schema registry; add a CI step that runs a backward/forward compatibility check on every producer PR — fail the build if the change breaks any registered consumer schema
Require producer teams to post a Slack message in #data-contracts at least 24 hours before deploying a schema change, so consumers have time to update their code
Use strong typing in the producer's application code (e.g., Avro or Protobuf classes); if the producer compiles without errors, the schema is compatible with all consumers
Run a nightly batch job that compares the current live schema of each topic against a snapshot taken 24 hours earlier; alert the on-call engineer if any columns were removed or renamed
explanation:
A schema registry with CI-enforced compatibility checks is the industry-standard operationalization of data contracts. Key properties: (1) schemas are version-controlled and discoverable; (2) compatibility rules (backward, forward, full) are machine-enforced, not dependent on human communication; (3) the check runs at PR time, before deployment — breaking changes are blocked at the source rather than detected after consumers fail. Tools like Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue Schema Registry, or a Git-hosted JSON Schema repo with a compatibility CLI all implement this pattern.

Option B (Slack notification) is informal and not enforceable — it depends on producers remembering to post and consumers reading it in time. It doesn't prevent accidental breaking changes.

Option C (producer compilation) checks the producer's own types, not consumer compatibility. A producer can rename a field in a way that compiles cleanly on its side but breaks every downstream consumer that expects the old name.

Option D (nightly diff) detects breaking changes after the fact — potentially 23+ hours after deployment. At that point, downstream consumers have already been failing for nearly a day.
hints: The goal is to prevent breaking changes from being deployed, not just to detect them after the fact. Which option blocks the change at the source?
Human coordination (Slack, email) is not a contract. A contract is machine-enforced.

title: Avro Consumer Failing After Producer Adds Required Field Without Default
scenario_context:
A Kafka producer pushes Avro-encoded events to a schema registry running BACKWARD compatibility mode. A producer team ships schema v2, which adds a required field `loyalty_tier` (type: string, no default value). Existing consumer services still use schema v1.

Consumer error log:
  ERROR AvroDeserializer — Failed to deserialize at offset 4820192
  org.apache.avro.AvroTypeException: Found user_events, expecting user_events,
  missing required field loyalty_tier
    at org.apache.avro.io.ResolvingDecoder.action(ResolvingDecoder.java:290)
    at org.apache.avro.io.ResolvingDecoder.readIndex(ResolvingDecoder.java:261)

Schema registry audit:
  Schema v2 accepted: BACKWARD compatibility check PASSED
  Reason logged: 'new field added' (compatibility check did not verify default presence)
description: The schema registry accepted the new schema but consumers are now failing. What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
options: BACKWARD compatibility mode allows adding fields only when they have a default value; schema v2 passed the registry's check because the registry's BACKWARD validator has a bug that omits the default-value requirement — the fix is to switch to FULL compatibility mode, which enforces stricter validation

The registry accepted the schema because BACKWARD compatibility only guarantees that new consumers can read old data — it says nothing about old consumers reading new data. A required field without a default value cannot be deserialized by old consumers holding schema v1 (they have no value to substitute for the missing field). The fix is to add a default value to `loyalty_tier` (e.g. `"unknown"`) so that schema v1 readers can safely skip or default the field when deserializing v2 messages.
The consumer is caching an outdated schema ID; restarting consumer instances forces them to re-fetch schema v2 from the registry and the deserialization error resolves without any schema change

Avro BACKWARD compatibility guarantees that consumers on any prior schema version can always read messages encoded with the new schema; the error indicates a network partition between the consumer and the schema registry, preventing schema resolution
explanation: BACKWARD compatibility means new schema readers can read data written with the OLD schema. The BACKWARD check verifies that schema v2 (the new reader) can deserialize messages encoded with schema v1 (old data) — that check passed correctly here, because v2 adds a field rather than removing or narrowing one. What BACKWARD does NOT guarantee is the reverse direction: old readers (v1 consumers) reading data written with the new schema (v2 messages). For that direction, any new field in v2 must carry a default value — when an old consumer encounters a v2 message, the new field is present in the wire data but absent from the old reader schema; Avro uses the field's default to fill the gap. Without a default, Avro's resolving decoder cannot construct a valid object for the old reader and throws `AvroTypeException: missing required field`. The registry's BACKWARD validator confirmed only the new-reader-reads-old-data direction and did not enforce the default-value requirement needed for old readers to safely deserialize new messages (that reverse guarantee falls under FORWARD compatibility). Fix: add `"default": "unknown"` to the `loyalty_tier` field definition in the Avro schema, then re-register the schema — existing consumers can now safely default missing fields when reading v2 messages. Option A is wrong — FULL compatibility adds bidirectional checks, but the core fix is the missing default, not the compatibility mode. Option C is wrong — restarting consumers makes them aware of the new schema, but the deserialization still fails without a default because their reader schema (v1) lacks the field. Option D is wrong — BACKWARD compatibility does NOT guarantee old readers can always read new data; it is specifically about new readers reading old data, and the old-reader-reads-new-data direction is exactly what failed here.
hints: BACKWARD compatibility is directional: new readers can read old data. What does that imply for old readers encountering a new field they have never seen?
When an old Avro reader encounters a field present in the written data but absent from its own schema, what does it use to substitute a value — and what happens when that substitution is impossible?

title: Backfill Job Producing Duplicate Rows in the Warehouse
scenario_context:
A data engineer runs a backfill to reprocess 30 days of daily metrics after a bug fix in the aggregation logic. After the backfill completes, downstream reports show exactly doubled metrics for every date in the backfill range.

Backfill script:
  for date in date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-01-30"):
      df = compute_daily_metrics(date)
      df.write \
        .mode("append") \
        .partitionBy("date") \
        .parquet("s3://warehouse/daily_metrics/")

Post-backfill audit:
  SELECT date, COUNT(*) as row_count, SUM(revenue) as total_revenue
  FROM daily_metrics
  WHERE date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-30'
  GROUP BY date
  ORDER BY date

  date        row_count   total_revenue
  2024-01-01  20,481      $2,014,882    ← expected ~10,240 rows / ~$1,007,441
  2024-01-02  19,988      $1,931,004    ← 2× expected
  ...         (all 30 dates doubled)
description: What is the root cause of the duplicates, and what is the correct fix for the backfill?
options: The backfill ran compute_daily_metrics in parallel across dates; concurrent Spark writers racing to write the same partition directory created duplicate Parquet files — adding .repartition(1) before the write serializes output and prevents the race condition

mode("append") adds new rows alongside existing rows in each date partition without checking whether data for that date already exists; since the original data was already present from the first pipeline run, the backfill appended a second full copy of each day. The correct mode for replacing existing partition data is mode("overwrite") combined with spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "DYNAMIC") so that only the backfilled date partitions are replaced, leaving other partitions untouched.

The partitionBy("date") clause caused Spark to write each day's output as a new Parquet file inside the existing date directory rather than replacing the existing file; enabling overwrite mode without DYNAMIC partition mode would have deleted the entire table, so append was the correct choice

The doubling is caused by compute_daily_metrics including both the original and corrected logic in the same DataFrame due to a union left in the code; the write mode is correct and the fix is to remove the union from the aggregation function
explanation: The root cause is using `mode("append")` on a table that already contains data for those date partitions. Spark's `append` mode adds new files to the existing partition directories without any awareness of existing data — it never reads or deduplicates against what is already there. After the backfill, every date partition contains both the original run's Parquet files and a new set of files from the backfill run; all downstream readers see both sets as part of the same partition, producing 2× row counts and 2× revenue totals. The correct approach is `mode("overwrite")` with `spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=DYNAMIC`. DYNAMIC overwrite mode tells Spark to replace only the partitions present in the current DataFrame, leaving all other date partitions untouched. STATIC overwrite (the default) would replace the entire table root, deleting all date partitions not in the current write — also wrong. Option A is wrong — concurrent writes to a partitioned S3 path do not cause row duplication (different dates write to different S3 prefixes); the issue is sequential append, not a race condition. Option C is wrong — `partitionBy` writes into the partition subdirectory; Spark never automatically replaces existing files unless overwrite mode is specified. Option D is wrong — the doubling matches exactly 2× the expected count for all 30 dates, which is the fingerprint of a double-write, not a union bug.
hints: append mode never removes or replaces existing files — it only adds new ones. What does that mean when the partition you are writing to already contains data from a previous run?
To replace only the partitions being written without touching historical data, which mode and which configuration setting are both required?

title: Consumer Lag Grows Unboundedly During Traffic Spike
scenario_context:
A Kafka-backed event pipeline processes clickstream events and writes enriched records to a warehouse. Under normal load (50K events/min), consumer lag stays below 10,000 events. During a marketing campaign, traffic spikes to 400K events/min for 4 hours. Consumer lag grows from 10K to 2.4 million events and never recovers after the spike ends, even 6 hours later.

Consumer metrics during spike:
  Events/min ingested by Kafka : 400,000
  Events/min processed by consumer: 48,000
  Consumer group size: 8 instances
  Kafka topic partitions: 8
  Processing time per event: 4–6 ms (unchanged from normal load)
  Consumer CPU: 12% average
  Downstream warehouse write latency: 380 ms avg (up from 22 ms normal)
description: What is the primary reason consumer lag is not recovering, and what is the correct intervention?
options: The 8-consumer group is limited to 8 partitions; adding more consumer instances beyond 8 has no effect. The 380 ms warehouse write latency is the true bottleneck — each consumer is serializing writes, so effective throughput is 1,000 ms / 380 ms ≈ 2.6 events/sec per consumer. The fix is to batch warehouse writes (accumulate records per micro-batch before flushing) or make writes async so network I/O does not block event consumption.

The consumer group lacks a rebalance trigger; after the spike, Kafka keeps all 8 partitions assigned to 8 consumers even if some are idle. Running a rolling restart forces Kafka to rebalance and redistribute lag evenly, allowing recovery.

The 2.4 million event backlog exceeds Kafka's default retention window; unread messages are expiring and will never be processed — the lag metric shows the cumulative count of dropped messages rather than unread messages
Consumer CPU at 12% indicates the bottleneck is in Kafka's broker-side log compaction, not the consumer; pausing log compaction on the topic during recovery allows full consumer throughput
explanation: The consumer group has 8 instances matched to 8 partitions — horizontal scaling is already saturated (you cannot add useful consumers beyond the partition count). The real bottleneck is the downstream warehouse write latency spiking from 22 ms to 380 ms. With synchronous writes, each consumer event-loop iteration blocks for 380 ms waiting for the warehouse to acknowledge the write before polling the next record. At 380 ms per event, maximum throughput per consumer is ~2.6 events/sec, or ~1,250 events/min for the group — far below the 50K/min normal load, let alone 400K/min peak. The 6-hour post-spike non-recovery confirms the write latency remained elevated, keeping throughput throttled. Interventions: (1) batch writes — accumulate N events before flushing to the warehouse so the per-event write cost is amortized; (2) async writes — decouple Kafka consumption from warehouse writes with an in-process buffer so polling continues while writes complete. Option B is wrong — a rolling restart triggers rebalance, but rebalancing partitions among the same 8 consumers does not change throughput when the bottleneck is write latency, not partition assignment imbalance. Option C is wrong — Kafka default retention is 7 days; a 4-hour spike does not approach that threshold, and consumer lag measures unread (retained) messages, not dropped ones. Option D is wrong — log compaction runs asynchronously on the broker and does not affect consumer poll throughput.
hints: Consumer CPU at 12% rules out compute saturation. Processing time per event is unchanged, so the problem is not the transformation logic. What remains in the per-event pipeline that could be blocking?
If the warehouse takes 380 ms to acknowledge each write and writes are synchronous, what is the maximum number of events a single consumer can process per minute?

title: Choosing the Right Data Contract Enforcement Tier
description: A data platform team wants to prevent breaking schema changes from silently reaching downstream consumers. They are evaluating three enforcement mechanisms: (A) schema registry with compatibility mode enforced at publish time, (B) automated contract tests in the producer's CI pipeline that assert field presence and type, (C) data observability platform with anomaly detection on schema drift post-ingestion. Which statement best characterizes the role each mechanism plays?
options: Schema registry catches structural format violations at publish time (before any consumer sees the message); CI contract tests catch breaking changes before code is merged (preventing bad schemas from ever being deployed); observability platforms catch schema drift that bypasses both static checks — such as a field being present but populated with NULLs or unexpected values in production. These three tiers are complementary, not substitutes.

Schema registry and CI contract tests are redundant — both validate the schema at development time; a single tier (the schema registry) is sufficient since it is the authoritative enforcement point and covers all scenarios

Data observability platforms provide the strongest guarantee because they observe real production data rather than synthetic test data; schema registries and CI tests should be replaced by observability tooling as the platform matures

CI contract tests are only relevant when the producer and consumer teams share a code repository; cross-team schema contracts must rely exclusively on the schema registry since CI pipelines cannot be coordinated across organizational boundaries
explanation: Each enforcement tier operates at a different point in the delivery lifecycle and catches a distinct class of failure. The schema registry enforces structural format rules at the moment a new schema version is published — it stops incompatible wire format changes before any message is produced. CI contract tests run during the pull-request review cycle, catching breaking changes before they are deployed — they can assert richer semantics than registry compatibility rules (e.g., specific fields required, value domain constraints, nullable guarantees). Observability platforms run continuously against live data, catching runtime drift that static analysis cannot detect: a field may be structurally present (passing registry and CI checks) but populated with NULLs, wrong enumerations, or shifted statistical distributions. None of these tiers can substitute for the others. Option B is wrong — the schema registry catches format incompatibility; CI tests catch semantic contract violations; they operate on different representations (schema metadata vs. actual data produced by the application logic). Option C is wrong — observability is a safety net, not a preventative gate; by the time observability alerts, bad data has already been ingested and may have propagated downstream. Option D is wrong — CI contract tests can be run by the producer team independently as a lint/test step; they do not require shared repository access or cross-team pipeline coordination.
hints: Think about when each mechanism fires: at schema publication, at code merge, or after data is in production. Which failures can only be caught at each stage?
A field that passes schema compatibility checks (it is present with the right type) can still carry semantically wrong values. Which tier is designed to catch that class of failure?

title: EU Data Residency: Preventing Cross-Region PII Replication
scenario_context:
A global data platform stores user events from EU and US users in a single centralized data lake in us-east-1. The legal team identifies a GDPR data residency requirement: EU user data must never leave EU storage regions. The current architecture replicates all raw events to the central lake before any regional filtering is applied.

Current pipeline:
  EU Kafka brokers → us-east-1 S3 raw zone → Spark processing → us-east-1 DWH
